Commonly reported barriers included financial concerns, worries about potential side effects, and limited knowledge about RSV and its vaccines. Trust in healthcare professionals and government authorities was commonly recognized as a facilitator. Additional facilitators included the availability of fee waivers or subsidies, access to more comprehensive vaccine information, and influence from community members, family, and friends. Knowledge gaps, safety concerns, financial considerations, and social influence were recurring themes in RSV vaccination decision-making, while trust in healthcare providers and government authorities was a salient facilitator. Future research should apply behavioural frameworks to design and evaluate targeted interventions that can be scaled within Hong Kong’s healthcare system.

title: AI-driven IMU-based monitoring system for detecting dry powder inhaler misuse
abstract: Inhaler misuse has been a persistent challenge for achieving effective pulmonary drug delivery with dry powder inhalers. Among the various misuse patterns, improper device maneuvering, especially incorrect device orientation, is one frequently overlooked yet clinically relevant misuse that impairs therapeutic efficacy. Currently, effective methods for timely and reliable detection of such misuse remain limited. To address this gap, we developed an AI-powered, motion-based digital monitoring system that could detect orientation-related misuse and other commonly observed inhaler-use errors. Specifically, a digital monitoring module was integrated into a Breezhaler ® device using inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors to capture orientation and movement signals during inhaler use. The collected data were processed and analyzed using two feature selection strategies, Boruta and Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation (RFECV), which were, for the first time, jointly applied to IMU-derived inhaler motion data to identify the most discriminative features. These selected features were then modeled using five machine learning algorithms: AdaBoostClassifier, ExtraTreesClassifier, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), XGBClassifier, and LogisticRegression. The analyses identified distinct optimal feature sets under Boruta (100 features) and RFECV (66 features) strategies, and revealed differences in model performance across predefined inhalation-related activities. The best-performing models, ExtraTrees classifier with Boruta and SVC with RFECV, illustrated excellent performance with accuracy of 0.967 and 0.950, respectively, as evaluated under a five-fold cross-validation scheme. Furthermore, SHAP-based interpretability analysis was conducted to elucidate feature importance and model decision patterns. In summary, this study demonstrates the feasibility of leveraging machine learning for accurate recognition and classification of inhalation activities and highlights the potential of this approach for future application in improving inhaler use and adherence.

title: Respiratory syncytial virus disease burden among adults in community and primary care settings in high-income countries: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and modelling study
abstract: Existing reports of RSV disease burden in adults focus primarily on hospitalisation while little is known about RSV disease burden in community and primary-care settings. In this study, we aimed to estimate RSV-associated acute respiratory infection (ARI) disease burden in community and primary-care settings among adults in high-income countries. We conducted a systematic literature review (PROSPERO registration: CRD42022377741) to identify published studies on RSV morbidity and mortality burden in community (including ill adults seeking or not seeking health care identified by prospective cohort studies with active case ascertainment) or primary-care settings (including outpatient and emergency department, ED) in adults in high-income countries. We accounted for the potential case under-ascertainment of RSV related to the imperfect test sensitivity of respiratory specimens and diagnostic tests by applying correction factors to the reported incidence rate and positive proportion estimates in individual studies. We estimated incidence rate and RSV positive proportion among those tested with acute respiratory illness by age group and setting. Random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to synthesise the estimates across studies. A total of six studies contributed to RSV incidence rate estimates in community or primary-care settings. The adjusted RSV incidence rate in the community was similar between persons aged 18–49 years (6104/100,000 person-years, 95% CI: 3737–9971; 1 study) and ≥ 50 years (5311/100,000 person-years, 95% CI: 3690–7643; 2 studies). In the outpatient setting, the adjusted RSV incidence rate increased with age, ranging from 2231/100,000 person-years (95% CI: 1088–4577; 2 studies) in adults aged 18–49 years to 4079/100,000 person-years (95% CI: 2759–6031; 3 studies) person-years in adults aged ≥ 65 years. Based on 1 study, RSV incidence rate in the ED was comparable between those aged 18–49 years (309/100,000, 142–676) and 50–64 years (300/100,000, 98–919), and was higher in adults aged ≥65 years (685/100,000 person-years, 95% CI: 258–2058). Based on five studies, the adjusted RSV positive proportion in adults with ARI was generally similar across the community, outpatient, and ED settings (range: 3.7–5.1%). This study revealed substantial RSV disease burden in community and primary-care settings across all age strata of adults in high-income countries. Compared to adults under age 65 years, older adults have higher RSV incidence rates in the ED and slightly higher incidence rates in the outpatient setting. These findings highlight the importance of considering RSV disease burden in community and primary-care settings when anticipating the potential impact of RSV vaccination.

title: Treatment responses to different inhalation therapies in GOLD 2026 group E patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a stratified analysis
abstract: The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2026 report revised the combined chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) assessment. Patients with one or more exacerbations in the past year are classified into group E, and long-acting β 2 -agonist (LABA) + long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) + or LABA + LAMA + inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) is recommended as initial inhalation therapy. However, COPD is a heterogeneous disease, and relying solely on exacerbation history may not capture its complexity. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to evaluate the treatment responses to different inhalation therapies in group E patients after stratified analysis based on the forced expiratory volume in the first second percentage of predicted (FEV1%pred), COPD Assessment Test (CAT), and exacerbations in the past year. This was a retrospective cohort study. Patients with COPD in group E (≥1 moderate/severe exacerbation) registered in the RealDTC study between January 2017 and June 2023 were enrolled. Patients were classified into FEV1%pred < 50% and FEV1%pred ≥ 50% groups, CAT < 10 and CAT ≥ 10 scores groups, non-frequent exacerbators and frequent exacerbators groups. Subsequently, all groups were subdivided into four groups: LAMA, LABA + ICS, LABA + LAMA, and LABA + LAMA + ICS. The number of future exacerbations, frequent exacerbations and hospitalizations, and all-cause mortality were collected during one year of follow-up. A total of 3911 patients were enrolled. During one year of follow-up, there were no significant differences in future exacerbations, frequent exacerbations and hospitalizations, and all-cause mortality among LAMA, LABA + LAMA, LABA + ICS, and LABA + LAMA + ICS in the FEV1%pred ≥ 50%, CAT < 10 scores, and non-frequent exacerbators groups. However, patients treated with LABA + LAMA or LABA + LAMA + ICS had a lower incidence of future exacerbations and frequent exacerbations than patients treated with LAMA or LABA + ICS in the FEV1%pred < 50%, CAT ≥ 10 scores, and frequent exacerbators groups ( P < 0.05). Although the GOLD 2026 report uniformly recommends LABA + LAMA or LABA + LAMA + ICS as initial inhaled regimens for group E patients, our stratified real-world findings partially diverge from this unified recommendation. Further individualized stratification based on FEV1%pred, CAT scores, and exacerbations in the past year may be beneficial to optimize initial inhalation therapy selection for heterogeneous group E patients.

title: Incident COPD in Belgian primary care: Exacerbation profiles, treatment patterns and opportunities to advance guideline concordant care
abstract: Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. International guidelines emphasize individualized care and timely treatment escalation, but evidence on local real-world implementation in primary care is limited. Methods This is a secondary data analysis of Intego, a Flemish primary care registry comprising anonymized electronic health records from 108 practices. Adults aged ≥40 years with a first-ever COPD diagnosis between January 2022 and December 2023 were included. Outcomes were initial pharmacological treatment, escalation to triple therapy after moderate exacerbations, and documentation of key clinical parameters and vaccinations. Results Among 1789 patients (mean age 67 years; 46.5% female), 44% experienced ≥1 exacerbation and 8.3% were frequent exacerbators (mean follow-up of 1.56 years). All-cause mortality was 8.9%, rising to 11.4% in frequent exacerbators. Spirometry was recorded in only 3.5%, and eosinophil counts were missing in 41.6%. Vaccination coverage was suboptimal (influenza 51%, pneumococcal 16%, COVID-19 77%). Only 9.8% of patients received LABA + LAMA at the time of diagnosis, 30.7% received LABA + ICS and 32.4% had no registered long-acting inhaled therapy at all. Escalation to triple therapy after an exacerbation occurred in 27.7% of patients with exacerbations (218/786), with a median delay of 65 days. Separately, among all patients exposed to triple therapy at any time during follow-up (n = 492), 217 (44.1%) experienced ≥1 moderate exacerbation after triple therapy was initiated. Conclusion COPD management in Flemish primary care shows major gaps in documentation, preventive care, and adherence to guideline-recommended pharmacological strategies. Delayed escalation and persistent exacerbations indicate system-level opportunities to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize treatment, and strengthen preventive measures.

title: Duration of pre-existing anxiety, depression or chronic analgesic use and associations with emergency lung cancer diagnosis and pre-diagnostic chest-imaging activity
abstract: Pre-existing conditions may influence emergency cancer diagnosis risk and decisions on investigations for potential cancer symptoms. In this retrospective cohort study we investigated whether the duration of pre-existing Anxiety/Depression and chronic analgesic use was associated with emergency lung cancer diagnosis and pre-diagnostic chest-imaging activity. We used linked primary care, hospital records and cancer registration data in patients with lung cancer. Pre-existing Anxiety/Depression and chronic analgesic use were categorised as recent-onset (first recorded <12months pre-cancer diagnosis) or long-term (first recorded >12months and <72months pre-diagnosis). Multivariable logistic regression explored associations between duration of Anxiety/Depression or chronic analgesic use and i) lung cancer diagnosis following Emergency Presentation (EP), and ii) use of Chest X-Ray/CT 1–6months pre-diagnosis. Among 6650 lung cancer patients, 26% had anxiety/depression (9% recent-onset) and 39% chronic analgesic use (28% recent-onset). Long-term and recent-onset chronic analgesic use were associated with reduced odds of EP (OR = 0.26; 95%CI 0.20, 0.33 and OR = 0.60; 95%CI 0.52, 0.70, respectively) versus no analgesic use. Pre-existing Anxiety/Depression were not associated with EP. Long-term chronic analgesic use was associated with increased odds of chest-imaging 1–6months pre-diagnosis (OR = 1.33; 95%CI 1.11, 1.60), versus no analgesic use. No associations were found for imaging use with recent-onset analgesics nor Anxiety/Depression. Long-term analgesic use for painful conditions was associated with lower odds of EP and higher odds of pre-diagnostic chest-imaging. This is consistent with a possible surveillance effect, whereby long-term conditions offer opportunities for diagnosing cancer before it becomes a medical emergency. Paying attention to symptomatic patients with no long-term treatment for painful conditions and ensuring appropriate follow up may help to expedite cancer diagnosis and avoid EP.

title: Allergic rhinitis in primary care: Navigating diagnostic uncertainty, treatment failure and referral
abstract: Allergic rhinitis is usually first recognised and treated in primary care, where decisions often precede allergen testing or specialist assessment. The challenge is not simply identifying classic allergic symptoms, but distinguishing clinically relevant allergy from sensitisation, nonallergic rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis and structural disease; selecting treatment according to burden; and recognising when apparent treatment failure reflects poor adherence, incorrect intranasal spray technique or an alternative diagnosis. This practice-oriented Review translates current guideline and consensus evidence into a decision sequence for first-contact care. It focuses on when a clinical diagnosis is sufficient, when targeted skin-prick or serum allergen-specific IgE testing will change management, how to optimise intranasal treatment, and how to separate allergy/immunology from otolaryngology referral pathways. The aim is to reduce indiscriminate testing, unnecessary treatment escalation and delayed referral while preserving the longitudinal advantages of primary care.

title: Influenza infection in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of global prevalence and association with exacerbations
abstract: Influenza infection is a potential contributor to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) morbidity, particularly during exacerbations. However, reported prevalence and its association with exacerbations vary across studies. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to estimate the prevalence of influenza in COPD and exacerbated COPD patients and to evaluate its association with exacerbations. Random-effects models with logit transformation were used to pool prevalence estimates and odds ratios (ORs). Subgroup analyses were performed by influenza type and subtype, patient setting, data collection period, and geographic region. Heterogeneity and publication bias were assessed using standard methods. A total of 50 studies on COPD, 44 studies on exacerbated COPD, and 4 case-control studies were included. The pooled prevalence of influenza was 10.6% (95% CI: 8.2–13.3% and I² = 98.7% for overall COPD and 95% CI: 8.4–13.2% and I² = 93.7% for exacerbated COPD) in both COPD and exacerbated COPD populations. Influenza A was the predominant type, followed by influenza B and C. Among subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2 showed comparable prevalence. The pooled OR for the association between influenza and exacerbation of COPD was 1.08 (95% CI: 0.48–2.46), indicating no significant association. Subgroup analyses by patient setting, temporal analysis, and geographic region did not demonstrate statistically significant differences. The pooled estimates should therefore be interpreted as averages across heterogeneous settings rather than as universally applicable prevalence values. Evidence regarding an association with COPD exacerbation remains inconclusive.

title: Pulmonary rehabilitation in a humanitarian context: a feasibility study from Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh
abstract: Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) is an effective intervention for chronic respiratory diseases (CRD), but its feasibility in low-resource and humanitarian settings remains underexplored. We evaluated a culturally adapted PR programme delivered across refugee camp health facilities, primary-care Upazila Health Complexes, and a District General Hospital in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. We conducted a single-arm mixed-methods feasibility study with assessments at baseline, eight weeks, and six months among adults with CRD participating in an 8-week PR programme comprising supervised exercise, self-management education, and psychosocial support. The primary outcome was exercise capacity measured using the Endurance Shuttle Walk Test (ESWT). Secondary outcomes included health status (COPD Assessment Test [CAT]), breathlessness (modified Medical Research Council [mMRC] Dyspnoea Scale), and psychological wellbeing (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale [HADS-A and HADS-D]). Of 91 individuals screened, 50 were enrolled (80% COPD; 20% asthma), yielding a recruitment rate of 54.9%. Adherence to supervised sessions was 100%, and follow-up completion was 98%. Participants had a mean age of 61.7 years (SD 10.1), and 50% were women. Significant improvements were observed across all outcomes (all p < 0.001). Mean ESWT endurance time increased from 181.5 s at baseline to 303.6 s at 8 weeks and 396.2 s at 6 months. Mean CAT scores improved from 23.8 to 11.1, mMRC scores from 2.9 to 1.1, HADS-A scores from 10.2 to 4.9, and HADS-D scores from 11.3 to 4.5 over 6 months. A culturally adapted PR programme was feasible and acceptable in a humanitarian setting and was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in exercise capacity, respiratory symptoms, health status, and psychological wellbeing. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate PR within a refugee camp setting. These findings provide important preliminary evidence to inform the integration of rehabilitation into humanitarian and primary healthcare systems and support further evaluation in controlled effectiveness and implementation studies.

title: Ecosocial environments and chronic lower respiratory disease mortality: a nationwide ecological study
abstract: Chronic lower respiratory disease (CLRD) is a leading cause of death in the United States and imposes a substantial economic burden. Ecosocial environments are closely linked to population health, yet nationwide evidence on their associations with CLRD mortality remains limited. This ecological study analyzed a longitudinal county-year panel of U.S. counties from 2014–2020. The primary outcome was the annual number of CLRD deaths among adults aged 55 years and older, obtained from the CDC Underlying Cause of Death database. Annual measures of four county-level ecosocial environments (food environment index, access to exercise opportunities, preventable hospital stays, and primary care physician density) were obtained from the County Health Rankings & Roadmaps program. Associations were estimated using quasi-Poisson models with a population offset, year fixed effects, and county-level cluster-robust standard errors. Models were progressively adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental and behavioral covariates, and exposures were examined both continuously and by quartiles. Robustness was assessed through stratified analyses, within-between decomposition, state fixed-effects models, spatially lagged X models, and time-lagged models. In fully adjusted models, a more favorable food environment index (RR = 0.96 [0.94–0.98] per 1 SD) and greater access to exercise opportunities (RR = 0.98 [0.96–0.99]) were associated with lower county-level CLRD mortality, whereas elevated preventable hospital stays were associated with higher mortality (RR = 1.05 [1.03–1.06]). These associations varied by sex and urbanization and were accounted for predominantly by between-county differences. They remained consistent in spatially lagged and time-lagged analyses, although the association for access to exercise opportunities was no longer significant after inclusion of state fixed effects. More favorable county-level food and exercise environments, as well as lower rates of preventable hospital stays, were associated with lower county-level CLRD mortality among middle-aged and older adults.

title: Risk factors of post-COVID-19 symptoms, a cross-sectional study in patients with asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease
abstract: Post-COVID-19 symptoms are common following COVID-19, but risk factors of persistent symptoms in patients with asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) remain unclear. We aimed to assess the frequency and risk factors of post-COVID-19 symptoms in patients with asthma and COPD. In this cross-sectional study, we used data from the Swedish PRAXIS study collected in 2022. The cohort included randomly selected adult patients with a diagnosis of asthma or COPD in medical records from central Sweden’s primary and secondary care. Participants completed a comprehensive questionnaire, and their responses were analysed. We used logistic regression and adjusted for age and lung disease diagnoses. Among 494 patients with confirmed COVID-19, 59% (289/494) reported post-COVID-19 symptoms. Risk factors for post-COVID-19 symptoms included severe acute infection (adjusted odds ratio aOR: 8.91, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.49–22.8), higher age (aOR:1.25, 95% CI: 1.09–1.45), female sex (aOR: 1.52, 95% CI: 1.04–2.21), and obesity [BMI ≥ 30] (aOR: 2.24, 95% CI: 1.44–3.47)). Anxiety/depression (aOR:1.79, 95% CI: 1.13–2.80) and chronic pain (aOR: 3.61, 95% CI: 1.95–6.69) were also significant risk factors. Patients with asthma or COPD had a high prevalence of post-COVID-19 symptoms compared to other studies. Several demographic and clinical factors were associated with post-COVID-19 symptoms, which could help identify patients at increased risk.

title: Acceptability of a mobile spirometry model for COPD case-finding in primary care: A qualitative exploration of patient and general practice perspectives
abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is among the top ten causes of death in Singapore, yet spirometry - the gold standard for diagnosis - remains significantly underutilized in primary care. We introduced a mobile health (mHealth) technology-based model for COPD case-finding in Singapore primary care, including a questionnaire for COPD risk stratification and referral to mobile spirometry using a digital platform. We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured, individual in-depth interviews with 20 patients at risk of COPD and 10 general practitioners (GPs) who referred patients to enrol in this new model. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and thematically analysed using deductive and inductive strategies, informed by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) framework. We found that GPs and patients generally perceived the new model as useful and acceptable, particularly for its ability to improve accessibility, increase awareness of COPD, and facilitate early detection. However, barriers related to the interpretation of spirometry results, workflow integration, the physical demands of the test, and psychological readiness among patients may influence its broader implementation. These results suggest that the new model for COPD case-finding has the potential to strengthen early detection of COPD and improve preventive respiratory care in Singapore primary care. However, barriers need to be addressed through system integration, training, and patient education to support future implementation.

title: Healthcare professionals’ perspectives and experiences of relief treatment for mild asthma in UK primary care settings
abstract: In 2024, the UK British Thoracic Society/National Institute for Health and Care Excellence/Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (BTS/NICE/SIGN) guidelines introduced a major change in asthma management, recommending inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/formoterol combination inhaler therapy as Anti-Inflammatory Reliever (AIR) or Maintenance and Reliever Therapy (MART) as the preferred treatment in patients with mild asthma over maintenance inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) with a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) reliever. This qualitative study was conducted within the RELIEF pragmatic randomised controlled trial to explore healthcare professionals’ (HCPs) experiences of prescribing ICS plus ICS/formoterol reliever (intervention) compared to ICS plus a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) reliever (control; treatment as usual) in patients with mild asthma. This study aimed to assess the acceptability and feasibility of switching patients’ current SABA reliever inhalers to ICS/formoterol reliever inhalers from a HCP perspective. Semi-Structured interviews were conducted with 30 HCPs across 28 primary care practices in the United Kingdom. Using thematic analysis, five overarching themes were constructed that provide insight into the barriers and facilitators to adopting changes in mild asthma management: mild asthma as a low-priority condition; medication beliefs and steroid-related concerns as barriers to implementation; acceptability and usability of combined inhalers in real-world practice; health literacy, education and persistent knowledge gaps; and patient-centred, flexible models of care as key implementation facilitators. Findings suggest that coordinated strategies encompassing patient and HCP education, prescribing support tools and structured review processes could mitigate behavioural, cultural and organisational barriers to new asthma guideline adherence.

title: A mixed-methods assessment of inhaler sustainability across the respiratory care pathway
abstract: Inhalers are central to asthma and COPD care but contribute to the environmental impact of respiratory services. Sustainability efforts have often focused on reducing device-level carbon emissions, particularly through switching from pressurised metered-dose inhalers to lower-carbon alternatives. However, the factors shaping sustainability across the wider respiratory care pathway are poorly understood. This study used a convergent mixed-methods design, informed by socio-technical systems theory, to examine inhaler sustainability across the UK respiratory care pathway. Qualitative interviews were conducted with patients, healthcare professionals, policymakers, industry representatives, and sustainability experts (n = 29). In parallel, surveys were administered to patients to explore inhaler appearance and recognition (n = 65) and to healthcare professionals to examine disposal and recycling practices (n = 76). Findings suggest that interconnected factors, including device design, regulation, prescribing systems, patient usability, and end-of-life infrastructure, shape inhaler sustainability. Sustainability was typically secondary to clinical considerations in prescribing decisions, and recycling pathways were poorly integrated into routine care. These findings highlight the need for whole-system approaches to improving inhaler sustainability while maintaining clinical safety, usability, and equitable respiratory care.

title: Factors contributing to over-prescription of short-acting β2-agonists (SABA) inhalers in patients with asthma in Hong Kong: a qualitative study on primary care physicians’ perspective
abstract: To explore primary care physicians’ perceptions of factors contributing to over-prescription of short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) inhalers in patients with asthma in a public primary healthcare setting in Hong Kong. TDF-informed qualitative interview study using individual semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis. 17 primary care physicians from the Department of Family Medicine and Primary Health Care in the New Territories West Cluster (NTWC) of Hospital Authority (HA) in Hong Kong were recruited and interviewed. Purposive sampling was adopted to ensure diversity of views. Inductively derived themes and subthemes describing perceived determinants of over-prescription of SABA inhalers, mapped deductively onto TDF domains. 4 major themes with 12 subthemes were identified: (1) knowledge of over-prescription of SABA inhalers, (2) balancing risks and benefits, (3) professional role and responsibility, and (4) environmental constraints. Physicians reported awareness of adverse outcomes associated with over-prescription of SABA inhalers but described knowledge gaps regarding usage thresholds; they perceived potential benefits of optimizing SABA inhaler prescription for benefits of patients and healthcare system yet feared of insufficient provision of reliever, patient confusion with new regimens, and strain on doctor–patient relationships. Participants saw themselves as gatekeepers responsible for guideline-concordant, evidence-based prescribing and patient education, but reported significant barriers from limited consultation time and lack of patient-friendly educational materials. Primary care physicians perceived that knowledge gaps, patient expectations, professional responsibilities, and environmental constraints were associated with over-prescription of SABA inhalers in public primary care setting in Hong Kong. These findings identify potential targets for future interventions.

title: Association of preserved ratio impaired spirometry and restrictive spirometric pattern with incident atrial fibrillation: a cohort study
abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation (AF). To our knowledge, no studies have examined the association of preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm) or restrictive spirometric pattern (RSP) with incident AF. We included participants without prevalent AF who had incident AF ascertainment and available spirometry and excluded those with airflow limitation. PRISm and RSP were evaluated as binary exposures and as four mutually exclusive spirometric patterns. Missing covariates were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations, and logistic regression estimates were pooled using Rubin’s rules. Sensitivity analyses used an individual lower limit of normal (LLN) for the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1 )/forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio, complete-case analysis, and an alternative smoking model including pack-years and current smoking. A total of 2219 participants were included, with a mean age of 62.4 years, of whom 43.6% were male. During follow-up, 247 incident AF events (11.1%) were recorded. In fully adjusted models, PRISm was associated with incident AF (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.12, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.35–3.31, P = 0.001), and RSP was also associated with incident AF (aOR = 2.38, 95% CI 1.58–3.60, P < 0.001). When participants were categorized into four mutually exclusive groups, PRISm+RSP remained associated with incident AF (aOR = 2.62, 95% CI 1.63–4.22, P < 0.001), whereas PRISm alone (aOR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.21–2.81, P = 0.690) and RSP alone (aOR = 1.88, 95% CI 0.93–3.80, P = 0.077) were not statistically significant. Results were consistent in sensitivity analyses. Among adults without airflow limitation, binary PRISm and RSP were associated with higher odds of incident AF. In mutually exclusive analyses, the clearest association was observed in participants with concurrent reductions in FEV 1 and FVC.

title: Evaluating influenza-related short videos on Chinese platforms: information quality, user engagement, and public health implications
abstract: Influenza-related short videos have become an important source of health information on Chinese social media. In an ongoing “information disorder” environment, where digital misinformation is known to cause health harms, their information quality and influenza-specific public health implications on major short-video platforms remain insufficiently characterized. On October 7, 2025, new accounts were registered to search for short videos on TikTok and Bilibili using the keywords “流感” (influenza) and “流行性感冒” (influenza) respectively. Basic information was extracted from each video, and quality was assessed using JAMA, GQS, modified DISCERN, and PEMAT, which do not verify factual accuracy. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software. A total of 229 influenza-related short videos were included, primarily uploaded by doctors (n = 73, 31.9%) and non-professional individuals (n = 88, 38.4%). Disease knowledge constituted the main video content (n = 176, 76.9%), with treatment being the primary video theme(n = 85, 37.12%), and monologue the predominant video format (n = 84, 36.68%). Compared to Bilibili, TikTok videos featured shorter lengths, more recent upload dates, higher counts of likes, comments, and shares, and were posted by creators with larger fans counts (all P < 0.001). Bilibili scored significantly higher than TikTok on both JAMA (2.5 (2, 3)) and GQS (4 (4, 4)) scales (both P < 0.001); while TikTok scored higher on PEMAT comprehensibility (100 (82, 100)) and executability (67 (0, 67)) (both P < 0.001). Videos from physicians, news agencies, and non-profit organizations, and those focusing on treatment or diagnosis, generally showed higher quality. The four quality scales were positively correlated(all P < 0.05), while correlations between quality scores and engagement metrics were weak. In the context of ongoing information disorder, influenza-related short videos have become a major channel for public health information access, yet the overall quality of this content remains suboptimal, with deficiencies in key clinical and preventive points. Improving short-form science communication will require higher-quality content, stronger platform governance, and enhanced public media literacy.

title: Assessment of teachers’ knowledge, awareness, and response to students with asthma in Greater Cairo schools
abstract: Bronchial asthma remains a significant public health challenge, especially among school-aged children. Schoolteachers are often the initial responders to asthma attacks, making their role vital for early symptom recognition and first aid provision. Therefore, this study aimed to explore the knowledge, awareness, and response of schoolteachers to students with asthma. Between March 2024 and October 2024, a self-administered questionnaire was created on Google Forms and distributed to schoolteachers through WhatsApp groups of private and public schools across different districts in Greater Cairo. The questionnaire consisted of three sections assessing: (1) teachers’ experience and demographics, (2) basic knowledge of asthma, and (3) knowledge related to first aid response in an asthma attack. A total of 634 schoolteachers participated in the study. Of these, 361 (57%) reported having previously taught students with bronchial asthma, whereas only 176 (27.8%) had witnessed a student having an acute asthma attack before. A majority of participants (445/634, 70.2%) correctly identified the short-acting beta agonist (SABA) inhaler or nebulizer as appropriate first aid for an acute asthma attack. However, only 187/634 (29.5%) reported knowing the correct technique for using SABA inhalers or nebulizers during an asthma attack. More than half of the participants, 362/634 (57.1%), provided appropriate answers regarding the etiology of the disease, specifically whether it was a contagious disease or not. There was no statistically significant association between teachers’ knowledge level and their sociodemographic characteristics. Teachers in Greater Cairo demonstrated fair knowledge and awareness regarding asthma. However, they did not fully understand appropriate first-aid responses, a gap that underscores the need for more asthma education programs.

title: 3Cs-Based intervention to improve influenza and pneumococcal vaccination in COPD patients: An RCT
abstract: To explore the impact of integrated medical and preventive interventions—comprising vaccine health promotion materials and a “vaccine health prescription” designed based on the 3Cs vaccine hesitancy model, led by CDC departments and implemented by hospital respiratory physicians—on the knowledge levels and vaccination rates of influenza vaccine (InfV) and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV) among COPD patients. Using convenience sampling, we recruited COPD patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria from the respiratory outpatient department of Guizhou Provincial People’s Hospital from June 2025 to January 2026 as study subjects. Inclusion criteria: (1) Aged ≥18 years and meeting COPD diagnostic criteria (post-bronchodilator FEV 1 /FVC < 0.70) with exclusion of other diseases; (2) Permanent residents of Guiyang City (referring to both registered and non-registered residents who have resided for more than half a year); (3) Meet the indications for InfV and/or PPV vaccination; (4) Voluntarily participate in the research and sign the informed consent form. Exclusion criteria: (1) Patients with contraindications to vaccination; (2) Patients who are unable to complete the questionnaire or refuse to participate in the study; (3) Patients who were vaccinated with InfV in 2025 and with PPV during the period from 2021–2025. A medical-prevention integrated intervention strategy designed by the Guizhou Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention based on the 3Cs vaccine hesitancy model, and implemented by respiratory outpatient doctors at Guizhou Provincial People’s Hospital.Outpatient doctors collected relevant information from COPD patients through questionnaires. Patients were randomly assigned to the control group and the intervention group. Vaccine hesitancy refers to the behavior of delaying or refusing vaccination when vaccines are available. The 3Cs model of vaccine hesitancy includes three dimensions: Confidence, Complacency, and Convenience. Confidence refers to the level of trust that individuals have in the safety and efficacy of vaccines, the healthcare system, and policymakers; Complacency refers to the perception that one is at low risk of infection, or the underestimation of the risk of vaccine-preventable diseases, leading individuals to believe that vaccination is unnecessary; Convenience refers to the accessibility of vaccination, including geographical reach, economic cost, service hours, and ease of procedures.The intervention group received vaccine health education based on the 3Cs model and were recommended a “vaccine health prescription” for receiving InfV and PPV. The control group did not receive the aforementioned interventions. A second questionnaire survey was conducted by telephone one month after the patient was enrolled. Query the actual administration of InfV and PPV within 6 months after patient enrollment through the vaccination service system. The primary outcomes observed were InfV and PPV vaccination rates, hesitancy rates, and changes in the three dimensions of the 3Cs model. Of the 265 initially enrolled subjects, 9 were lost to follow-up (3.4%), leaving 256 for analysis (128 in each group). Post-intervention, hesitancy rates for InfV were significantly lower in the experimental group than in the control group (21/128 vs 45/128), hesitancy rates for PPV were significantly lower in the experimental group than in the control group (31/128 vs 60/128) ; vaccination rates for InfV were significantly higher in the experimental group than in the control group(54/128 vs 12/128), PPV vaccination coverage within the previous 5 years were significantly higher in the experimental group than in the control group(42/128 vs 12/128). title: Principles for a patient-centred transition to low-global warming potential pressurised metered-dose inhalers
abstract: Pressurised metered-dose inhalers (pMDIs) are a common device type used to deliver various inhaled medicines to the lungs of patients with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other respiratory diseases. Most pMDIs use hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) propellants, such as hydrofluoroalkane (HFA)-134a, which is a powerful greenhouse gas with a 100-year global warming potential (GWP) 1530 times more potent than CO2. Legislation in developed countries, particularly in Europe, will reduce the availability of high-GWP propellants, enforcing the phase-down of HFC-containing pMDIs within the next five years. Inhaler manufacturers are at various stages of research and development and regulatory approval to reformulate pMDIs with next-generation propellants (HFA-152a, hydrofluoroolefin (HFO)-1234ze[E]) with a much lower carbon footprint. If the transition is not carefully managed, there are risks to patient health. From the patient perspective, the transition must be seamless. Here we aim to provide a clear, consensus-based framework to deliver this transition. Following a policy roundtable which included stakeholders across the respiratory community, four key principles were outlined: (1) patient safety and seamless continuity of access; (2) securing supply through shared responsibility and collaboration across the respiratory community; (3) alignment of regulatory and policy interventions across jurisdictions; (4) building trust through credible, clinician-centred communication. These principles prioritise patient health, while recognising the need to balance environmental commitments as we transition from current to low-GWP inhalers. This framework serves as a call to action, and we encourage all respiratory stakeholders to use the principles as a foundation for external discussions with policymakers and regulators.
